guide.title: Unit 6: Consequences of Industrialization: review guide
guide.intro: Industrial states sought raw materials, markets, and prestige, and between 1750 and 1900 they expanded their empires across Africa, Asia, and the Pacific. This unit covers the justifications and methods of imperialism, the many forms of resistance, the growth of a global economy, and the migrations that industrialization set in motion.

sections.title: Rationales and expansion
body: Imperialists justified expansion with ideas such as the “civilizing mission,” Social Darwinism, and racial hierarchy, as well as with economic and strategic arguments. Industrial technology (steamships, railroads, the telegraph, quinine against malaria, and rapid-fire guns) made conquest easier.

European states divided most of Africa after the Berlin Conference (1884–1885); Britain extended its rule over India after 1858; the United States annexed the Philippines in 1898; and Japan took Taiwan (1895) and Korea (1910). Some states, such as Russia and the United States, also expanded across neighboring land.
points: Separate justifications (ideas) from means (technology) and motives (economic needs).
Settler colonies, such as Australia, differed from colonies ruled by small administrations.

sections.title: Resistance and reform
body: Resistance took many forms: armed revolt (the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the Zulu wars, Ethiopia's victory over Italy at Adwa in 1896), religious movements (the Ghost Dance, the Xhosa cattle killing), and political organization (the Indian National Congress, founded in 1885).

Writers such as Dadabhai Naoroji criticized the economic “drain” of wealth from India to Britain. Some states, such as the Ottoman Empire during the Tanzimat reforms and Meiji Japan, reformed and modernized in order to resist outside pressure.
points: Ask whether resistance aimed to restore old ways, reform, or win independence.
Causation questions often link industrial needs to both expansion and resistance.

sections.title: The global economy and migration
body: Colonies and independent states alike shifted toward exporting raw materials, such as cotton from Egypt and India, rubber from the Congo, and beef from Argentina, to industrial countries. Britain fought the Opium Wars (1839–1842 and 1856–1860) to force China to open trade, and imposed unequal treaties. Some historians call this economic imperialism.

Millions migrated: Irish families fleeing famine, Italians to Argentina and the United States, and Chinese and Indian indentured laborers to the Caribbean, Southeast Asia, and Africa. Receiving societies often reacted with restrictions such as the U.S. Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) and the White Australia policy, while migrants built ethnic enclaves.
points: Explain push factors (famine, poverty) and pull factors (jobs, land).
Economic imperialism could control a country without formally ruling it.

example.prompt: Explain one way industrialization caused imperial expansion.
example.solution: Factories needed raw materials such as cotton and rubber and new markets for their goods, so industrial states sought colonies or controlled trade with weaker states; technologies such as steamships and rapid-fire guns made that expansion easier.

misconceptions: Nationalism, religion, prestige, and racial ideas also drove expansion.
Resistance was widespread, from armed revolts to political movements.
“Indentured servitude was the same as slavery.”
Indentured workers signed contracts for a set term, though conditions could be harsh and coercive.
Countries such as China and Argentina were shaped by foreign economic power without becoming colonies.

passages.title: Source A: Rudyard Kipling, “The White Man's Burden,” 1899
text: “Take up the White Man's burden— / Send forth the best ye breed— / Go, bind your sons to exile / To serve your captives’ need; / To wait, in heavy harness, / On fluttered folk and wild— / Your new-caught sullen peoples, / Half devil and half child.”
passages.attribution: Rudyard Kipling, British writer, first stanza of a poem published in 1899 urging the United States to take control of the Philippines. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax World History, Volume 2, section 9.2.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (written in English and published in 1899). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax World History, Volume 2 (openstax.org/books/world-history-volume-2/pages/9-2-motives-and-means-of-imperialism); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source B: Two American views of annexing the Philippines, 1900
text: Source 1, Senator Albert Beveridge, speech in the U.S. Senate, January 1900: “The Philippines are ours forever . . . And just beyond the Philippines are China’s illimitable markets. We will not retreat from either. . . . Our largest trade henceforth must be with Asia. The Pacific is our ocean. . . . Where shall we turn for consumers of our surplus? Geography answers the question. China is our natural customer.”

Source 2, Negro National Democratic League, Address to the Public, July 1900: “We hold that the policy known as imperialism is hostile to liberty and leans toward the destruction of government by the people themselves. . . . A nation cannot oppress a people without the borders of the country without sooner or later introducing some such oppression within its borders.”
passages.attribution: A speech by a U.S. senator from Indiana, and a public statement by an African American political organization, both 1900. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax World History, Volume 2, section 9.3.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (the Senate speech is printed in the Congressional Record, a U.S. government publication, and the League's address was published in 1900). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax World History, Volume 2 (openstax.org/books/world-history-volume-2/pages/9-3-colonial-empires); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source C: Dadabhai Naoroji, “The Benefits of British Rule,” 1871
text: “Politically: Repeated breach of pledges to give the natives a fair and reasonable share in the higher administration of their own country, which has much shaken confidence in the good faith of the British word. . . . Financially: All attention is engrossed in devising new modes of taxation, without any adequate effort to increase the means of the people to pay . . . To sum up the whole, the British rule has been: morally, a great blessing; politically, peace and order on one hand, blunders on the other; materially, impoverishment, relieved as far as the railway and other loans go. The natives call the British system Sakar ki Churi, the knife of sugar. That is to say, there is no oppression, it is all smooth and sweet, but it is the knife, notwithstanding.”
passages.attribution: Dadabhai Naoroji, Indian merchant, scholar, and later a founder of the Indian National Congress, writing in English for a British audience, 1871. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax World History, Volume 2, section 9.4.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (written in English in 1871). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax World History, Volume 2 (openstax.org/books/world-history-volume-2/pages/9-4-exploitation-and-resistance); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of the global economy and migration, 1800–1900
text: “Steamships, railroads, the telegraph, and the Suez Canal, opened in 1869, knit the world into a single market. Industrial countries bought cotton from Egypt and India, rubber from the Congo, and beef and wheat from Argentina, and sold manufactured goods in return. When China restricted the opium trade, Britain fought the Opium Wars and imposed treaties that opened Chinese ports. The same networks moved people. Irish families fled famine; Italians sailed to Buenos Aires and New York; Chinese and Indian laborers signed contracts of indenture to work for years on plantations and railroads in the Caribbean, Southeast Asia, and East Africa. Receiving societies often pushed back, as in the U.S. Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.

questions.prompt: Source A presents imperial rule as
choices: a duty owed by the conquerors to the peoples they rule
a mistake that the conquerors should quickly undo by withdrawing
a partnership between equal peoples
a profitable business that requires no sacrifice
questions.explanation: Kipling calls empire a “burden” that requires the best sons to “serve your captives’ need”: the idea of a civilizing mission.
choiceExplanations: He urges readers to “Take up” the burden.
He describes the ruled as “captives,” not equals.
He stresses sacrifice (“exile,” “heavy harness”), not easy profit.

questions.prompt: The phrase “Half devil and half child” portrays colonized peoples as
choices: skilled rulers who should be left to govern themselves
equal partners in trade with the West
a military threat that must be destroyed
uncivilized and in need of guidance
questions.explanation: The phrase depicts colonized peoples as both wicked and immature, a racist justification for rule.
choiceExplanations: The poem denies their ability to govern.
The poem presents them as subordinate.
The poem calls for ruling, not destroying, them.

questions.prompt: The historical situation in which Source A was written is best described as
choices: U.S. debate over ruling the Philippines after the war with Spain
the end of European empires after World War II
the Berlin Conference's division of East Asia among the European powers and Japan
Britain's loss of its American colonies
questions.explanation: Kipling wrote in 1899, as the United States debated ruling the Philippines after the Spanish–American War.
choiceExplanations: The poem was written decades before decolonization.
The Berlin Conference concerned Africa.
The American Revolution ended in 1783.

questions.prompt: Which development most directly challenged the view of colonized peoples in Source A?
choices: The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869
The rapid spread of Kipling's poems in British schools
Filipino armed resistance to U.S. rule after 1899
The British government's decision to send more troops to India
questions.explanation: Filipino independence fighters' long armed resistance contradicted the image of passive peoples waiting for guidance.
choiceExplanations: The Suez Canal was a trade route.
The poem's popularity spread its view rather than challenging it.
Sending troops reflects imperial power, not a challenge to the poem's view.

questions.prompt: In Source 1, Beveridge's main economic reason for keeping the Philippines is
choices: access to Chinese markets for American goods
a plan to grow sugar for European markets
cheap Filipino labor for American factories and farms
the gold mines of the Philippine islands
questions.explanation: He calls China “our natural customer” and says the Philippines give a base near “China's illimitable markets.”
choiceExplanations: He looks to Asian, not European, markets.
He speaks of consumers, not laborers.
He does not mention gold.

questions.prompt: Source 2 opposes annexation chiefly on the grounds that
choices: the Philippines are too far away to defend
ruling other peoples betrays liberty and invites oppression at home
the islands have no value for American trade
annexation would cost American workers their jobs and lower their wages
questions.explanation: The League calls imperialism “hostile to liberty” and warns that oppression abroad will return “within its borders.”
choiceExplanations: Distance is not their argument.
They make a moral and political, not commercial, argument.
Jobs are not mentioned.

questions.prompt: Source 1 best illustrates which development of the late nineteenth century?
choices: Spain expanding its empire in the Pacific
The United States withdrawing from all foreign trade to protect its industries
The United States seeking overseas territory and markets
China colonizing islands in Southeast Asia
questions.explanation: After 1898 the United States took the Philippines and looked to Asian markets, as European powers and Japan were expanding too.
choiceExplanations: Spain lost the Philippines in 1898.
Beveridge calls for more trade, not withdrawal.
China was the target of trade, not a colonizer here.

questions.prompt: The League's position as an African American organization in 1900 best explains why Source 2
choices: argues that Filipinos are unfit to govern themselves
praises the federal government's policy in the American South
links oppression abroad to racial oppression at home
supports annexation as a duty of the white race
questions.explanation: The full address compares U.S. rule in the Philippines to white control of Black-majority areas of the South; the excerpt's warning about oppression “within its borders” reflects that experience.
choiceExplanations: It insists that all peoples are entitled to liberty.
The League criticizes conditions in the South.
It opposes the “White Man's burden” argument.

questions.prompt: Naoroji's main political complaint in Source C is that
choices: Indians had too much influence over British laws
Indians were denied a fair share in governing their own country
the British had refused to build any railways or roads in India
British rule had brought no peace or order to India
questions.explanation: He cites the “repeated breach of pledges to give the natives a fair and reasonable share in the higher administration.”
choiceExplanations: His complaint is the reverse: too little voice.
He mentions the railway as a partial relief.
He grants that British rule brought “peace and order.”

questions.prompt: When Naoroji describes British rule as “materially, impoverishment,” he means that
choices: India was poor before the British arrived and stayed the same
Britain sent large amounts of money to India
British rule made India's farmers rich
British rule made India poorer
questions.explanation: He judges British rule's material effect on India as impoverishment, the idea later called the “drain” of wealth.
choiceExplanations: He blames British rule for the impoverishment.
He argues that wealth flowed out of India, not into it.
That is the opposite of his claim.

choices: brought only benefits to Indians
was openly violent and cruel at every turn
was about to end because Indians had grown rich
seemed gentle while still causing real harm
questions.explanation: Naoroji explains that “it is all smooth and sweet, but it is the knife, notwithstanding.”
choiceExplanations: The image shows hidden harm.
He says “there is no oppression” on the surface; the harm is hidden.
Nothing suggests an end to British rule.

choices: defend British rule against Indian critics
persuade the British to reform their rule, not end it
call for an immediate armed revolt against British rule
ask another European power to replace Britain
questions.explanation: Writing in English for a British audience, he balances praise and criticism and appeals to British “fair play,” which reflects early reformist nationalism.
choiceExplanations: He criticizes British rule.
He calls for no revolt.
He addresses Britain, not another power.

choices: were enslaved for life with no contract
signed contracts to work for a set term
traveled only within their home countries
owned the plantations where they worked
questions.explanation: The source says laborers “signed contracts of indenture to work for years.”
choiceExplanations: Indentured labor was contract labor, not lifelong slavery.
They traveled overseas.
They worked on plantations; they did not own them.

a Chinese law banning emigration
a receiving society restricting immigration
a British law ending the opium trade
questions.explanation: The U.S. law barred most Chinese immigration, a reaction against migrants by a receiving society.
choiceExplanations: It restricted, rather than recruited, Chinese workers.
It was a U.S. law.
It had nothing to do with opium.

choices: economic imperialism: forcing a country open to trade
a successful Chinese effort to end all foreign trade
a migration caused by famine
China expanding its empire into Britain
questions.explanation: Britain fought to keep selling opium and imposed treaties that opened Chinese ports without making China a colony.
choiceExplanations: China was defeated and forced to open its ports.
The wars concerned trade, not famine.
China was the target of British pressure.

questions.prompt: Which development described in Source D did the most to make both imperial expansion and global trade possible?
choices: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882
The migration of Italians to Buenos Aires
The decline of demand for raw materials in the industrial countries
New technologies such as steamships, railroads, and the telegraph
questions.explanation: These technologies connected markets and made it easier to move goods, troops, and orders over long distances.
choiceExplanations: The act restricted migration; it did not enable trade.
Migration was a result of these connections.
Demand for raw materials rose.
